claim: The foveola covers the central 1.3 degrees of visual angle (dva).
source: The foveola covers the central 1.3 degrees of visual angle (dva) (Hendrickson, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hendrickson, 2005

claim: The fovea covers the central 5.5 dva.
source: The fovea and parafovea cover the central 5.5 and 8.3 dva, respectively (Hendrickson, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hendrickson, 2005

claim: The parafovea covers the central 8.3 dva.
source: The fovea and parafovea cover the central 5.5 and 8.3 dva, respectively (Hendrickson, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hendrickson, 2005

claim: Within the foveal pit, retinal layers spread aside and allow light to impinge directly onto a densely packed population of cone photoreceptors.
source: Within a small, central region of the retina known as the foveal pit, retinal layers spread aside and allow light to impinge directly onto a densely packed population of cone photoreceptors – the foveola (Hageman and Johnson, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hageman and Johnson, 1991

claim: More than 40% of primary visual cortex is devoted to the processing of foveal input even though the fovea covers merely the central 5 degrees of the visual field.
source: even though the fovea covers merely the central 5 degrees of the visual field, more than 40% of primary visual cortex is devoted to the processing of foveal input (Curcio et al., 1990; Tootell et al., 1988; Hendrickson, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Curcio et al., 1990; Tootell et al., 1988; Hendrickson, 2005

claim: Foveal processing appears understudied on both a neurophysiological and behavioral level.
source: Quite surprisingly, foveal processing appears understudied on both a neurophysiological and behavioral level (Schira et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schira et al., 2009

claim: Pre-saccadic sensitivity modulations at the target of eye movements have been characterized by decades of research.
source: In the moving observer in particular, decades of research have characterized pre-saccadic sensitivity modulations at the target of eye movements (Zhao et al., 2012; Squire et al., 2013; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhao et al., 2012; Squire et al., 2013; Li et al., 2021

claim: Little to nothing is known about the concurrent development of visual sensitivity in the pre-saccadic center of gaze.
source: To date, little to nothing is known about the concurrent development of visual sensitivity in the pre-saccadic center of gaze (Hanning and Deubel, 2022; Ludwig et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hanning and Deubel, 2022; Ludwig et al., 2014

claim: During fixation, the fovea contributes to the processing of stimuli presented in the periphery.
source: Evidence from neuroimaging (Williams et al., 2008; Fan et al., 2016), brain stimulation (Chambers et al., 2013), and psychophysics (Fan et al., 2016; Yu and Shim, 2016; Weldon et al., 2020) suggests that during fixation, the fovea contributes to the processing of stimuli presented in the periphery
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to neuroimaging, brain stimulation, and psychophysics studies

claim: Relevant peripheral objects are represented in foveal retinotopic cortex, possibly via feedback connections from temporal areas.
source: using functional magnetic resonance imaging, Williams et al., 2008; Fan et al., 2016 demonstrate that relevant peripheral objects are represented in foveal retinotopic cortex, possibly via feedback connections from temporal areas (Rockland and Van Hoesen, 1994; Bullier, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Williams et al., 2008; Fan et al., 2016; Rockland and Van Hoesen, 1994; Bullier, 2001

claim: Disrupting foveal processing through transcranial magnetic stimulation impairs peripheral discrimination performance.
source: Indeed, disrupting foveal processing through transcranial magnetic stimulation (Chambers et al., 2013) or the presentation of a foveal distractor (Fan et al., 2016; Weldon et al., 2020) impairs peripheral discrimination performance.
evidence: Supported by citation to Chambers et al., 2013

claim: The presentation of a foveal distractor impairs peripheral discrimination performance.
source: Indeed, disrupting foveal processing through transcranial magnetic stimulation (Chambers et al., 2013) or the presentation of a foveal distractor (Fan et al., 2016; Weldon et al., 2020) impairs peripheral discrimination performance.
evidence: Supported by citations to Fan et al., 2016; Weldon et al., 2020

claim: Saccade preparation is accompanied with an obligatory shift of attention to the saccade target.
source: First and foremost, saccade preparation is accompanied with an obligatory shift of attention to the saccade target (Zhao et al., 2012; Squire et al., 2013; Li et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhao et al., 2012; Squire et al., 2013; Li et al., 2021

claim: The shift of attention to the saccade target has been shown to decrease foveal sensitivity.
source: saccade preparation is accompanied with an obligatory shift of attention to the saccade target (Zhao et al., 2012; Squire et al., 2013; Li et al., 2021) which in turn has been shown to decrease foveal sensitivity (Hanning and Deubel, 2022; Ludwig et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hanning and Deubel, 2022; Ludwig et al., 2014

claim: The execution of a rapid eye movement induces brief motion signals on the retina.
source: Moreover, the execution of a rapid eye movement induces brief motion signals on the retina (Castet et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to Castet et al., 2002

claim: Foveal receptive fields are challenging to estimate in neurophysiological investigations since even in paralyzed monkeys, gaze is never fully stable.
source: in neurophysiological investigations, foveal receptive fields are challenging to estimate since even in paralyzed monkeys, gaze is never fully stable (Forte et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Forte et al., 2002

claim: Recent developments combining a free viewing approach with an offline reconstruction of visual input allow for estimations of foveal receptive fields.
source: Only recent developments combining a free viewing approach with an offline reconstruction of visual input allow for these estimations (Yates et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yates et al., 2021

claim: Congruent False Alarm rates exceeded incongruent ones.
source: Indeed, congruent False Alarm rates (FARs) exceeded incongruent ones.
evidence: Based on experimental data from Experiment 1

claim: Target-congruent and incongruent FAs relied on an incidental, high energy of the reported orientation in the foveal noise.
source: Target-congruent and incongruent FAs indeed relied on an incidental, high energy of the reported orientation in the foveal noise.
evidence: Based on analysis of foveal noise properties in Experiment 1

claim: Enhancement was most pronounced in the center of gaze and exhibited an asymmetric profile, extending further towards than away from the target.
source: Enhancement was most pronounced in the center of gaze and exhibited an asymmetric profile, extending further towards than away from the target.
evidence: Based on experimental data from Experiment 2

claim: Congruent and incongruent HRs did not differ in the baseline.
source: Congruent and incongruent HRs did not differ in the baseline (HRcong-incong = – 0.7 ± 8.5%; p=0.589)
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Congruent and incongruent HRs did not differ in the earliest pre-saccadic bin.
source: Congruent and incongruent HRs did not differ in the baseline (HRcong-incong = – 0.7 ± 8.5%; p=0.589) and earliest pre-saccadic bin (HRcong-incong = – 0.7 ± 5.1%; p=0.669).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: HRs for congruent probes significantly exceeded HRs for incongruent probes throughout the remaining bins after the earliest pre-saccadic bin.
source: Afterwards, a stable congruency effect emerged: HRs for congruent probes significantly exceeded HRs for incongruent probes throughout the remaining bins (HRcong-incong=6.0 ± 5.7%, 7.0 ± 6.5%, 6.4 ± 3.8%, 5.9 ± 5.2%, for the time bins [–200 –150[, [–150 –100[, [–100 –50[, [–50 0[ ms, respectively; all ps <0.003).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: When generating a FA, observers reported the target orientation more often than the non-target orientation.
source: When generating a FA, observers reported the target orientation more often than the non-target orientation, leading to higher congruent than incongruent FARs (FARcong-incong=5.9 ± 3.3%; p<0.001; Figure 2B).
evidence: Based on experimental data from Experiment 1

claim: Noise images associated with target-congruent FAs were characterized by a high energy around the target orientation.
source: Noise images associated with target-congruent FAs were characterized by a high energy around the target orientation. The identified cluster exhibited a center of mass (CM) close to +45° (oriCM = 39.38°, SFCM = 0.86 cycles per degree (cpd); tSum = 6625.7; p<0.001).
evidence: Based on analysis of foveal noise properties

claim: The cluster of high energy around the target orientation included SFs from .67 cpd to 1.19 cpd.
source: Interestingly, this cluster included SFs from.67 cpd to 1.19 cpd – a range that covers the pre-saccadic development of visual resolution at the target of a 10 dva saccade (Kroell and Rolfs, 2021).
evidence: Based on analysis of foveal noise properties and citation to Kroell and Rolfs, 2021

claim: The cluster encompassing higher SFs manifested exclusively during saccade preparation.
source: Indeed, separating noise images that had appeared before or after target onset revealed that the cluster encompassing higher SFs manifested exclusively during saccade preparation (oriCM = 40.31°, SFCM = 0.57 cpd; tSum = 22,099.0; p<0.001; Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: Based on analysis of foveal noise properties separated by time

claim: Noise images associated with target-incongruent FAs exhibited a high energy around the perceived, non-target orientation.
source: Noise images associated with target-incongruent FAs exhibited a high energy around the perceived, non-target orientation. The corresponding cluster was slightly repelled from the target orientation (oriCM = 60.0°) and confined to very low SFs from.33 to.51 cpd (SFCM = 0.41 cpd; tSum = 5587.7; p =< 0.001).
evidence: Based on analysis of foveal noise properties

claim: The underlying noise images for incongruent FAs exhibited an absence of evidence for the target orientation that manifested in a cluster of low energy centered on 41.25°.
source: Instead, the underlying noise images exhibited an absence of evidence for the target orientation that manifested in a cluster of low energy centered on 41.25° (SFCM = .68 cpd; tSum = –20,050; p=0.002).
evidence: Based on analysis of foveal noise properties

claim: The total amount of evidence necessary to trigger incongruent FAs exceeded the evidence underlying congruent FAs by a factor of 3.4.
source: Since incongruent FAs required both, perceptual evidence for the non-target orientation and an absence of evidence for the target orientation, the total amount of evidence necessary to trigger incongruent FAs exceeded the evidence underlying congruent FAs by a factor of 3.4, p<0.001.
evidence: Based on analysis of foveal noise properties

claim: Enhancement was most pronounced in the center of gaze at –0.1±1.7 dva with a difference of 7.7 ± 4.8% between congruent and incongruent HRs.
source: While feature-based attention would predict a uniform detection advantage for congruent probes across all tested locations, the difference between the curves, and therefore enhancement, was most pronounced in the center of gaze (HRcong-incong=7.7 ± 4.8% at –0.1±1.7 dva; p<0.001).
evidence: Based on experimental data from Experiment 2

claim: Enhancement remained significant within a region of 6.4 dva around the pre-saccadic fixation, extending from –2.6 to +3.8 dva.
source: Enhancement remained significant within a region of 6.4 dva around the pre-saccadic fixation, extending further towards the saccade target than away from it: congruent HRs significantly exceeded incongruent ones from –2.6 to +3.8 dva.
evidence: Based on experimental data from Experiment 2

claim: The congruent HR profile exhibited a significantly higher peak than the incongruent one (87.9 ± 7.3% vs 80.4 ± 7.8%).
source: The congruent HR profile exhibited a significantly higher peak than the incongruent one (80.4 ± 7.8% vs 87.9 ± 7.3%, p<0.001, BF10=22.689).
evidence: Based on experimental data from Experiment 2

claim: The vertical offsets of the congruent and incongruent profile did not differ significantly.
source: At the same time, and in opposition to a global enhancement of target-congruent orientations, the vertical offsets of the congruent and incongruent profile did not differ significantly (39.3 ± 19.2% vs 35.9 ± 16.3%, p=0.323, BF10=0.340).
evidence: Based on experimental data from Experiment 2

claim: Congruent FARs significantly exceeded incongruent ones in Experiment 2 (9.4 ± 7.3%).
source: Again, congruent FARs significantly exceeded incongruent ones (FARcong-incong=9.4 ± 7.3%; p<0.001).
evidence: Based on experimental data from Experiment 2

claim: Incongruent HRs for parafoveal probes at -3 dva were statistically indistinguishable from incongruent HRs for probes presented in the center of gaze.
source: This manipulation was successful: incongruent HRs for parafoveal probes were statistically indistinguishable from incongruent HRs for probes presented in the center of gaze (–3 dva: 79.1±14.8% vs 81.3 ± 8.4%, p=0.489, BF10=0.400; 3 dva: 77.7±15.5% vs 81.3 ± 8.4%, p=0.415, BF10=0.435).
evidence: Based on experimental data from session 7 of Experiment 2

claim: Congruent and incongruent HRs did not differ for probes appearing away from the saccade target at -3 dva.
source: Even though performance had been raised to a foveal level, congruent and incongruent HRs differed neither for probes appearing away from (HRcong-incong=−3.7 ± 10.0%, p=0.127, BF10=0.531) nor towards (HRcong-incong=1.4 ± 9.0%, p=0.336, BF10=0.352) the saccade target
evidence: Based on experimental data from session 7 of Experiment 2

claim: Congruent and incongruent HRs did not differ for probes appearing towards the saccade target at +3 dva.
source: Even though performance had been raised to a foveal level, congruent and incongruent HRs differed neither for probes appearing away from (HRcong-incong=−3.7 ± 10.0%, p=0.127, BF10=0.531) nor towards (HRcong-incong=1.4 ± 9.0%, p=0.336, BF10=0.352) the saccade target
evidence: Based on experimental data from session 7 of Experiment 2

claim: For accurate saccades, enhancement reached significance between –2.6 and 2.1 dva and from 3.2 dva throughout the measured range towards the saccade target.
source: When probe locations were aligned to the center of gaze, considering only accurate saccades yielded significant enhancement from –2.6 to 2.1 dva and from 3.2 dva throughout the measured range towards the saccade target (Figure 3A).
evidence: Based on analysis of accurate saccades in Experiment 2

claim: For inaccurate saccades, enhancement reached significance between –1.1 and 4.4 dva.
source: Inaccurate saccades showed a more pronounced asymmetry (Figure 3B): enhancement reached significance between –1.1 and 4.4 dva.
evidence: Based on analysis of inaccurate saccades in Experiment 2

claim: Inaccurate saccades were hypometric on average (Mdn = 9.7 ± 0.4 dva).
source: Since inaccurate saccades were hypometric on average (Mdn = 9.7 ± 0.4 dva), asymmetric enhancement would have boosted congruency at the remapped target location across all trials.
evidence: Based on analysis of saccade endpoints in Experiment 2

claim: Aligning probe positions to the remapped target location on an individual-trial level did not lead to a narrowing of the enhancement profile.
source: Yet, aligning probe positions to the remapped target location on an individual-trial level did not lead to a narrowing of the enhancement profile (Figure 3C).
evidence: Based on analysis of remapping-aligned data in Experiment 2

claim: Congruency effects were more pronounced in Pre-Post trials than in Pre trials.
source: While we observed significant congruency effects when the target was visible exclusively during saccade preparation, congruency was more pronounced in Pre-Post trials (Figure 4): across all pre-saccadic time bins, the difference in HRs amounted to 2.5 ± 6.0% in Pre and to 6.9 ± 2.8% in Pre-Post trials, p<0.001.
evidence: Based on comparison of Pre and Pre-Post trials in Experiment 1

claim: When the target disappeared during the saccade, congruent HRs significantly exceeded incongruent ones in medium stages of saccade preparation.
source: Target foveation impacted the time course of congruency effects: when the target disappeared during the saccade, congruent HRs significantly exceeded incongruent ones in medium stages of saccade preparation ([–250 –200] ms: HRcong-incong=4.4 ± 4.9%; p=0.003; [–200 –150] ms: HRcong-incong=5.6 ± 7.7%; p=0.024; [–150 –100] ms: HRcong-incong=8.4 ± 7.6%; p<0.001).
evidence: Based on analysis of Pre trials in Experiment 1

claim: In Pre-Post trials, congruent HRs significantly exceeded incongruent HRs in all bins after the earliest bin.
source: In Pre-Post trials, congruent HRs numerically exceeded incongruent HRs throughout saccade preparation, though this difference failed to reach significance in the earliest bin (HRcong-incong=5.6 ± 7.5%; p=0.055). In all later bins, congruent HRs significantly exceeded incongruent HRs (HRcong-incong=7.6 ± 8.3%, 8.2 ± 8.3%, 3.8 ± 5.7%, 10.5 ± 9.5%; all ps <0.041).
evidence: Based on analysis of Pre-Post trials in Experiment 1

claim: Congruency was most pronounced in the window from 11 to 21ms post-saccadic target duration.
source: We determined the difference between congruent and incongruent HRs within a boxcar window (width: 10ms; step size: 1ms) sliding across the range of post-saccadic target durations (1–48ms). Congruency was most pronounced in the window from 11 to 21ms (HRcong-incong=9.1 ± 3.4%).
evidence: Based on analysis of post-saccadic target duration in Experiment 1

claim: The mean pre-saccadic congruency effect from Experiment 1 failed to reach significance during fixation (1.5 ± 4.7%).
source: In contrast to the mean pre-saccadic congruency effect from Experiment 1, the mean congruency effect during fixation failed to reach significance (1.5 ± 4.7%, p=0.277, BF10=0.378; Figure 5B).
evidence: Based on comparison of Experiment 1 and Experiment 3

claim: The magnitude of the pre-saccadic congruency effect significantly exceeded the mean congruency effect during fixation.
source: Across all probe presentation time points, the magnitude of the pre-saccadic congruency effect significantly exceeded the mean congruency effect during fixation, p=0.046.
evidence: Based on within-observer comparison of Experiment 1 and Experiment 3

claim: Pre-saccadic congruency effects reached significance when the probe was presented 100ms after the target.
source: Pre-saccadic congruency effects emerged rapidly: they reached significance when the probe was presented 100ms after the target (3.9 ± 4.7%, p=0.008) and peaked at a target-probe interval of 150ms (8.8 ± 7.6%, p<0.001).
evidence: Based on target-locked analysis of Experiment 1

claim: Pre-saccadic congruency effects peaked at a target-probe interval of 150ms.
source: Pre-saccadic congruency effects emerged rapidly: they reached significance when the probe was presented 100ms after the target (3.9 ± 4.7%, p=0.008) and peaked at a target-probe interval of 150ms (8.8 ± 7.6%, p<0.001).
evidence: Based on target-locked analysis of Experiment 1

claim: Congruency effects during fixation developed more slowly and only reached significance when the probe appeared 250ms after the target.
source: Congruency effects during fixation, in turn, developed more slowly and only reached significance when the probe appeared 250ms after the target (7.4 ± 8.6%, p=0.007; all remaining time points: ps >0.379; BF10s<0.425).
evidence: Based on target-locked analysis of Experiment 3

claim: Congruency effects in the saccade condition reached significance from the second to the last pre-saccadic time bin.
source: While congruency effects in the saccade condition reached significance from the second ([–200 –150[ ms) to the last ([–50 0[ ms) pre-saccadic time bin (all ps <0.003), congruency effects in the fixation condition failed to reach significance throughout (all ps >0.16).
evidence: Based on movement-locked comparison of Experiment 1 and Experiment 3

claim: Congruency effects in the fixation condition failed to reach significance throughout all pre-saccadic time bins.
source: While congruency effects in the saccade condition reached significance from the second ([–200 –150[ ms) to the last ([–50 0[ ms) pre-saccadic time bin (all ps <0.003), congruency effects in the fixation condition failed to reach significance throughout (all ps >0.16).
evidence: Based on movement-locked comparison of Experiment 1 and Experiment 3

claim: Defining features of an eye movement target are predictively enhanced in the pre-saccadic center of gaze.
source: We demonstrate that defining features of an eye movement target are predictively enhanced in the pre-saccadic center of gaze.
evidence: Based on the combined results of all experiments

claim: Foveal enhancement was both temporally and spatially specific.
source: Foveal enhancement was both temporally and spatially specific, more pronounced when the saccade target was foveated briefly after saccade landing and accelerated during saccade preparation as compared to fixation.
evidence: Based on the combined results of all experiments

claim: Foveal enhancement was more pronounced when the saccade target was foveated briefly after saccade landing.
source: Foveal enhancement was both temporally and spatially specific, more pronounced when the saccade target was foveated briefly after saccade landing and accelerated during saccade preparation as compared to fixation.
evidence: Based on comparison of Pre and Pre-Post trials in Experiment 1

claim: Foveal enhancement was accelerated during saccade preparation as compared to fixation.
source: Foveal enhancement was both temporally and spatially specific, more pronounced when the saccade target was foveated briefly after saccade landing and accelerated during saccade preparation as compared to fixation.
evidence: Based on comparison of Experiment 1 and Experiment 3

claim: Neurons in several temporal areas project back to primary visual cortex and potentially relay feature information about relevant peripheral stimuli to V1 neurons with foveal receptive fields.
source: For instance, neurons in several temporal areas (e.g. TE, IT, TPO, STS), most of which are associated with the computation of position-invariant object information, project back to primary visual cortex and potentially relay feature information about relevant peripheral stimuli to V1 neurons with foveal receptive fields (Rockland and Van Hoesen, 1994; Bullier, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rockland and Van Hoesen, 1994; Bullier, 2001

claim: Peripheral features can be decoded from brain activation in foveal – but not other peripheral – retinotopic areas.
source: Crucially, peripheral features can be decoded from brain activation in foveal – but not other peripheral – retinotopic areas (Williams et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Williams et al., 2008

claim: Encoding models based on deep convolutional neural networks used to predict neural responses to natural scene stimuli in a purely bottom-up fashion consistently fail to account for foveal activity in visual cortical areas.
source: Moreover, encoding models based on deep convolutional neural networks used to predict neural responses to natural scene stimuli in a purely bottom-up fashion consistently fail to account for foveal activity in visual cortical areas (Mell et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mell et al., 2021

claim: Neurons in temporal areas exhibit median response latencies of 50–130 ms.
source: An involvement of foveal feedback connections in saccade preparation appears physiologically feasible: neurons in the previously mentioned temporal areas exhibit median response latencies of 50–130 ms (Bullier, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bullier, 2001

claim: A foveal distractor no longer impacted peripheral discrimination performance when observers prepared a saccade away from the to-be discriminated object.
source: The only study investigating foveal feedback in an active setting revealed that a foveal distractor no longer impacted peripheral discrimination performance when observers prepared a saccade away from the to-be discriminated object (Fan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fan et al., 2016

claim: Pre-saccadic attention shifts to the eye movement target in an obligatory fashion.
source: During saccade preparation, this selection mechanism would emerge naturally: pre-saccadic attention shifts to the eye movement target in an obligatory fashion (Deubel and Schneider, 1996; Moore and Fallah, 2001)
evidence: Supported by citations to Deubel and Schneider, 1996; Moore and Fallah, 2001

claim: Pre-saccadic attention shifts faster than covert attention does.
source: Pre-saccadic attention shifts faster than covert attention does (Rolfs and Carrasco, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Rolfs and Carrasco, 2012

claim: Pre-saccadic attention uncrowds the saccade target from surrounding objects.
source: and even uncrowds the saccade target from surrounding objects (Harrison et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harrison et al., 2013

claim: In spontaneous visual behavior, gaze is directed to the currently most significant object in the scene.
source: Most importantly, pre-saccadic attention is a natural relevancy filter – in spontaneous visual behavior, gaze is directed to the currently most significant object in the scene (Einhäuser et al., 2008; Nuthmann and Henderson, 2010; 't Hart et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Einhäuser et al., 2008; Nuthmann and Henderson, 2010; 't Hart et al., 2013

claim: Saccades often exhibit post-saccadic oscillations, which are assumed to reflect residual pupil movement rather than a true rotation of the eyeball.
source: When recorded with pupil-based eye trackers, saccades often exhibit post-saccadic oscillations, which are assumed to reflect residual pupil movement rather than a true rotation of the eyeball (Nyström et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nyström et al., 2013

claim: Orientation discrimination performance during saccade preparation decreases in the fovea as it increases at the saccade target location.
source: Yet, our results are in line with the finding that, compared to fixation, orientation discrimination performance during saccade preparation decreases in the fovea as it increases at the saccade target location (Hanning and Deubel, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hanning and Deubel, 2022

claim: Coherent motion at the saccade target causes immediate ocular following upon saccade landing.
source: Coherent motion at the saccade target, for instance, causes immediate ocular following upon saccade landing (Kwon et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kwon et al., 2019

claim: High-level peripheral information such as object category has been successfully decoded from foveal neuronal activation.
source: The feedback mechanism itself seems capable of operating at this complexity: high-level peripheral information such as object category has been successfully decoded from foveal neuronal activation (Williams et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Williams et al., 2008

claim: Foveal feedback connections gain a predictive nature during saccade preparation.
source: We suggest a crucial contribution of foveal processing to transsaccadic visual continuity which, up until now, has been overlooked. Feedback connections to foveal retinotopic cortex, so far characterized during passive fixation, gain a predictive nature during saccade preparation
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results

claim: Feedback connections to foveal retinotopic cortex entail a retinotopic anticipation of soon-to-be foveated information without the need for predictive spatial updating.
source: they entail a retinotopic anticipation of soon-to-be foveated information – notably without the need for predictive spatial updating.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results showing enhancement aligned to center of gaze

claim: The predictive foveal enhancement of target features may contribute to the continuous perception of eye movement targets and accelerate post-saccadic gaze correction.
source: As a behavioral consequence, the predictive foveal enhancement of target features demonstrated here may contribute to the continuous perception of eye movement targets and accelerate post-saccadic gaze correction.
evidence: Based on speculation about functional implications of findings

claim: Foveal processing of saccade targets commences before the movement is executed and thereby enables a seamless transition once the center of gaze reaches the target.
source: Based on these findings, we suggest a crucial contribution of foveal processing to trans-saccadic visual continuity: Foveal processing of saccade targets commences before the movement is executed and thereby enables a seamless transition once the center of gaze reaches the target.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results

claim: The fovea is not simply a passive receiver of input for high-acuity vision.
source: We hypothesized that the fovea is not simply a passive receiver of input for high-acuity vision.
evidence: Based on hypothesis supported by experimental findings

claim: The fovea assumes a crucial role in the establishment of visual continuity across saccades.
source: Instead, it appears uniquely suited to predict incoming information and, in consequence, to assume a crucial role in the establishment of visual continuity across saccades.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results

claim: Already before an eye movement, critical features of the peripheral target should be available for foveal processing.
source: Foveal feedback, so far characterized during fixation, gains a predictive nature when applied to active vision: already before an eye movement, critical features of the peripheral target should be available for foveal processing.
evidence: Based on inference from foveal feedback literature applied to active vision

claim: Foveal feedback may facilitate post-saccadic target processing or gaze correction when the eyes land erroneously off-target.
source: Once gaze has shifted, the target is foveated. In the moving observer, foveal feedback therefore anticipates incoming information and may facilitate post-saccadic target processing or gaze correction when the eyes land erroneously off-target (Deubel et al., 1982; Ohl and Kliegl, 2016; Tian et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on inference supported by citations to Deubel et al., 1982; Ohl and Kliegl, 2016; Tian et al., 2013

claim: Feedback to the current center of gaze would suffice to predict the features of the eye movement target in retinotopic coordinates, irrespective of the future foveal location.
source: Most notably, this mechanism would not require predictive spatial updating to support transsaccadic continuity: irrespective of the future foveal location, feedback to the current center of gaze would suffice to predict the features of the eye movement target in retinotopic coordinates.
evidence: Based on inference about mechanism

claim: If foveal feedback remains effective during saccade preparation, fed-back information on the saccade target should combine with foveal input and thereby facilitate the detection of target-congruent, foveal feature information.
source: We hypothesized that, if foveal feedback remains effective during saccade preparation, fed-back information on the saccade target should combine with foveal input and thereby facilitate the detection of target-congruent, foveal feature information.
evidence: Based on hypothesis tested in experiments

claim: On a perceptual level, foveal feedback should correspond to a predictive enhancement of saccade target features in the pre-saccadic center of gaze.
source: On a perceptual level, this should correspond to a predictive enhancement of saccade target features in the pre-saccadic center of gaze.
evidence: Based on hypothesis tested in experiments

claim: Observers were able to select the peripheral stimulus as the saccade target.
source: Observers were able to select the peripheral stimulus as the saccade target
evidence: Demonstrated by saccade landing coordinates shown in Figure 1D

claim: Neither saccade latencies nor saccade endpoints influenced congruency effects.
source: Neither saccade latencies nor saccade endpoints influenced congruency effects (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Based on analysis described in Materials and methods

claim: Foveal HRs decreased continuously in the course of saccade preparation, when attention is known to shift to the target.
source: Irrespective of congruency, foveal HRs decreased continuously in the course of saccade preparation, when attention is known to shift to the target (Hanning and Deubel, 2022; Ludwig et al., 2014; Figure 2B; see Appendix 1—figure 1 for individual observer data).
evidence: Based on experimental data and citations to Hanning and Deubel, 2022; Ludwig et al., 2014

claim: Foveal HR was 86.5 ± 11.1% in the earliest pre-saccadic bin 250–200ms before saccade onset.
source: We observed a HR of 86.5 ± 11.1% in the earliest pre-saccadic bin 250–200ms before saccade onset and a significantly lower HR of 77.1 ± 6.8% 50–0ms before the saccade (bootstrapped p<0.001; see Materials and methods).
evidence: Based on experimental data from Experiment 1

claim: Foveal HR was significantly lower at 77.1 ± 6.8% in the 50–0ms bin before the saccade compared to the earliest pre-saccadic bin.
source: We observed a HR of 86.5 ± 11.1% in the earliest pre-saccadic bin 250–200ms before saccade onset and a significantly lower HR of 77.1 ± 6.8% 50–0ms before the saccade (bootstrapped p<0.001; see Materials and methods).
evidence: Based on experimental data from Experiment 1

claim: A pronounced increase in overall HRs occurred between the baseline and earliest pre-saccadic time point (69.7 ± 10.8% vs 86.5±6.7).
source: Moreover, we observed a pronounced increase in overall HRs between the baseline and earliest pre-saccadic time point (69.7 ± 10.8% vs 86.5±6.7, p<0.001).
evidence: Based on experimental data from Experiment 1

claim: Observers yielded similar incongruent HRs in the baseline and last pre-saccadic time bin (70.0 ± 8.8% vs 74.1 ± 7.0%).
source: Crucially however, observers yielded similar incongruent HRs in the baseline and last pre-saccadic time bin (70.0 ± 8.8% vs 74.1 ± 7.0%, p=0.152, BF10=0.503).
evidence: Based on experimental data from Experiment 1

claim: The increase in overall HRs between baseline and earliest pre-saccadic time point could be attributed to a predictive remapping of attention to the future retinotopic location of the saccade target.
source: This finding could be attributed to a predictive remapping of attention to the future retinotopic location of the saccade target – the fovea (Rolfs et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on inference supported by citation to Rolfs et al., 2011

claim: The onset of the target stimulus may have created an urgency signal that transiently lowered decision thresholds.
source: Yet another possibility is that the onset of the target stimulus created an urgency signal that transiently lowered decision thresholds (Thura et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on speculation supported by citation to Thura et al., 2012

claim: FAs are not time-resolved since observers may have perceived the probe at any time in the course of a probe-absent trial.
source: FAs are not time-resolved since observers may have perceived the probe at any time in the course of a probe-absent trial.
evidence: Based on logical inference about the nature of FA trials

claim: The range of SFs from .67 cpd to 1.19 cpd covers the pre-saccadic development of visual resolution at the target of a 10 dva saccade.
source: Interestingly, this cluster included SFs from.67 cpd to 1.19 cpd – a range that covers the pre-saccadic development of visual resolution at the target of a 10 dva saccade (Kroell and Rolfs, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kroell and Rolfs, 2021

claim: Information about the target was available for foveal processing at a resolution influenced by the target's pre-saccadic eccentricity.
source: This suggests that information about the target was indeed available for foveal processing, at a resolution influenced by the target's pre-saccadic eccentricity.
evidence: Based on inference from noise analysis results

claim: Fed-back information may have interacted with foveal noise content, allowing ori*SF combinations congruent with the fed-back signal to drive response behavior.
source: Fed-back information may have interacted with foveal noise content, allowing those ori*SF combinations that are congruent with the fed-back signal – but not others – to drive response behavior.
evidence: Based on inference from noise analysis results

claim: The low-SF portion of the cluster for incongruent FAs relied on images visible in the baseline time bin.
source: Whereas the low-SF portion of this cluster relied on images visible in the baseline time bin, the portion encompassing target-like orientations in a higher SF spectrum manifested exclusively during saccade preparation (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: Based on temporal analysis of noise properties

claim: Throughout the trial, noise content as target-dissimilar as possible was required for observers to perceive a competing orientation in the foveal noise.
source: Combined, the high-energy cluster repelled from the target orientation, and the low-energy cluster covering a wide SF range around the target orientation suggest that throughout the trial, noise content as target-dissimilar as possible was required for observers to perceive a competing orientation in the foveal noise.
evidence: Based on inference from noise analysis results

claim: The total amount of evidence necessary to trigger incongruent FAs exceeded the evidence underlying congruent FAs by a factor of 3.4.
source: Since incongruent FAs required both, perceptual evidence for the non-target orientation and an absence of evidence for the target orientation, the total amount of evidence necessary to trigger incongruent FAs exceeded the evidence underlying congruent FAs by a factor of 3.4, p<0.001.
evidence: Based on analysis of filter responses within identified clusters

claim: FAs constitute a systematic reaction to foveal visual input rather than classical FAs.
source: To summarize, just like Hits, FAs constitute a systematic reaction to foveal visual input. Rather than classical FAs, these responses therefore seem to constitute Hits triggered by stimulus information with a lower signal-to-noise ratio.
evidence: Based on inference from noise analysis results

claim: Congruency effects in FARs can be interpreted in the same way as congruency effects in HRs as reflecting an interaction between peripheral target information and congruent foveal input.
source: Congruency effects in FARs can be interpreted in the same way as congruency effects in HRs: information about the peripheral saccade target interacts with congruent foveal input and facilitates its detection.
evidence: Based on inference from noise analysis results

claim: The size of the stimulus used to probe performance will presumably determine the width of the enhancement profile.
source: Note that the size of the stimulus used to probe performance will presumably determine the width of the enhancement profile.
evidence: Based on inference about methodological considerations

claim: Enhancement may be confined to an even narrower region than the data indicate.
source: Since the probe stimulus in our experiment had a comparably large radius of 1.5 dva, the leftmost significant point at –2.6 dva could indicate enhancement of a probe centered on –1.1 dva (and thus covering the very center of gaze). Consequently, enhancement may be confined to an even narrower region than our data indicate.
evidence: Based on inference about methodological considerations

claim: Enhancement peaks in the center of gaze.
source: While the width of the enhancement profile should be interpreted with caution, the main conclusions that can be drawn are that enhancement (i) peaks in the center of gaze
evidence: Based on experimental data from Experiment 2

claim: Enhancement is not uniform throughout the tested spatial range as global feature-based attention would predict.
source: (ii) is not uniform throughout the tested spatial range as, for instance, global feature-based attention would predict
evidence: Based on experimental data from Experiment 2

claim: Enhancement is asymmetrical, extending further towards the saccade target than away from it.
source: and (iii) is asymmetrical, extending further towards the saccade target than away from it.
evidence: Based on experimental data from Experiment 2

claim: FAs were primarily triggered by foveal orientation information despite observers' explicit knowledge about the range of probe locations.
source: An inspection of noise properties revealed that – despite observers' explicit knowledge about the range of probe locations – FAs were primarily triggered by foveal orientation information (Supplements; Appendix 1—figure 7 and Appendix 1—Video 1).
evidence: Based on analysis of noise properties in Experiment 2

claim: Enhancement may depend on the baseline performance level at a given eccentricity.
source: Enhancement may depend on the baseline performance level at a given eccentricity.
evidence: Based on speculation about potential confound

claim: For hypometric horizontal saccades, the predictively remapped target location is shifted into the hemifield of the target by the magnitude of the undershoot.
source: To distinguish between both possibilities, we took advantage of the observation that the precise remapping vector depends on saccade endpoints on an individual-trial level (Collins et al., 2009): for hypometric horizontal saccades, the predictively remapped target location is shifted into the hemifield of the target by the magnitude of the undershoot (Figure 3C, top panel).
evidence: Supported by citation to Collins et al., 2009

claim: For hypermetric horizontal saccades, the predictively remapped target location is shifted into the opposite hemifield by the magnitude of the overshoot.
source: Conversely, for hypermetric horizontal saccades, the predictively remapped target location is shifted into the opposite hemifield by the magnitude of the overshoot.
evidence: Based on inference from Collins et al., 2009

claim: The spatial offset between the center of gaze and the remapped target location increases with saccadic landing error.
source: Since the spatial offset between the center of gaze and the remapped target location increases with saccadic landing error, we separated all recorded eye movements into 'accurate' (the saccade landed on the target stimulus, that is, no more than 1.5 dva from its center) and 'inaccurate' (the saccade landed off-target but within the accepted landing radius of 3.25 dva around it).
evidence: Based on inference about relationship between landing error and remapping

claim: An increase in asymmetry for inaccurate saccades could bear functional advantages since it would boost congruency at the remapped target location across all trials.
source: An increased asymmetry for inaccurate saccades may indeed be related to predictive remapping: since inaccurate saccades were hypometric on average (Mdn = 9.7 ± 0.4 dva), asymmetric enhancement would have boosted congruency at the remapped target location across all trials.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results

claim: The adjustment in asymmetry seems to rely on an estimate of average rather than single-trial saccade characteristics.
source: Importantly though, this adjustment seems to rely on an estimate of average rather than single-trial saccade characteristics: aligning probe locations to the remapped attentional locus on an individual trial level provides further evidence that, irrespective of individual saccade endpoints, enhancement was aligned to the fovea.
evidence: Based on inference from remapping-aligned analysis

claim: Irrespective of individual saccade endpoints, enhancement was aligned to the fovea.
source: aligning probe locations to the remapped attentional locus on an individual trial level provides further evidence that, irrespective of individual saccade endpoints, enhancement was aligned to the fovea.
evidence: Based on remapping-aligned analysis in Experiment 2

claim: A brief foveation of the target was sufficient to boost congruency.
source: A brief foveation of the target was sufficient to boost congruency. We determined the difference between congruent and incongruent HRs within a boxcar window (width: 10ms; step size: 1ms) sliding across the range of post-saccadic target durations (1–48ms). Congruency was most pronounced in the window from 11 to 21ms (HRcong-incong=9.1 ± 3.4%).
evidence: Based on analysis of post-saccadic target duration in Experiment 1

claim: Congruent and incongruent HRs were virtually identical for both Pre and Pre-Post trials in the baseline bin.
source: In the baseline bin, congruent and incongruent HRs were virtually identical for both Pre (HRcong-incong = –0.9 ± 9.8%, p=0.534) and Pre-Post (HRcong-incong = –0.4 ± 12.6%, p=0.590) trials.
evidence: Based on experimental data from Experiment 1

claim: Pre-saccadic congruency effects are more pronounced than congruency effects during fixation.
source: We conducted a third experiment to compare the magnitude and time course of pre-saccadic congruency effects from Experiment 1 to congruency effects during fixation.
evidence: Based on comparison of Experiment 1 and Experiment 3

claim: Pre-saccadic congruency effects develop faster than congruency effects during fixation.
source: We conducted a third experiment to compare the magnitude and time course of pre-saccadic congruency effects from Experiment 1 to congruency effects during fixation.
evidence: Based on comparison of Experiment 1 and Experiment 3

claim: Congruency effects during fixation are unlikely to be caused by small-scale oculomotor activity.
source: Since we did not observe a lateralization of fixation densities, congruency effects – if present – are unlikely to be caused by small-scale oculomotor activity.
evidence: Based on analysis of fixation densities in Experiment 3

claim: Saccade preparation entails the emergence of two spatially confined attention pointers: one centered on the saccade target and one centered on its predictively remapped location.
source: Saccade preparation entails the emergence of two spatially confined attention pointers (Cavanagh et al., 2010): one centered on the saccade target and one centered on its predictively remapped location, that is, the foveal region (Rolfs et al., 2011; Collins et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cavanagh et al., 2010; Rolfs et al., 2011; Collins et al., 2009

claim: The appearance of the saccade target may have introduced global feature-based attention to its orientation.
source: At the same time, the appearance of the saccade target in our investigation may have introduced global feature-based attention to its orientation (White and Carrasco, 2011).
evidence: Based on speculation supported by citation to White and Carrasco, 2011

claim: The fovea as the region of highest acuity may be assigned a permanent attention pointer.
source: It is conceivable that the fovea as the region of highest acuity is assigned a permanent attention pointer.
evidence: Based on speculation about attention mechanisms

claim: The joint modulation of spatial and feature-based attention could operate across the visual field and may underlie previous findings demonstrating an interaction of feature information between peripheral locations.
source: In principle, however, this mechanism could operate across the visual field and may underlie previous findings that demonstrate an interaction of feature information between peripheral locations [for motion discrimination (Szinte et al., 2016), crowding (Harrison et al., 2013), and adaptation (He et al., 2018; Biber and Ilg, 2011; Melcher, 2007)].
evidence: Based on speculation supported by citations to Szinte et al., 2016; Harrison et al., 2013; He et al., 2018; Biber and Ilg, 2011; Melcher, 2007

claim: Observers likely reported the presence of a target-congruent foveal probe whenever perceptual evidence for its orientation had exceeded a certain threshold.
source: Observers likely reported the presence of a target-congruent foveal probe whenever perceptual evidence for its orientation had exceeded a certain threshold.
evidence: Based on inference about decision mechanism

claim: Orientation information was sampled simultaneously from the foveal and peripheral attentional focus.
source: Assuming that orientation information was sampled simultaneously from the foveal and peripheral attentional focus, and assuming that the foci persisted for a brief period after saccade landing (Golomb, 2019; Jonikaitis et al., 2013), the salient post-saccadic foveal view of the target may have allowed even early and therefore subthreshold pre-saccadic foveal information to contribute to an above-threshold signal.
evidence: Based on speculation supported by citations to Golomb, 2019; Jonikaitis et al., 2013

claim: The attentional foci persisted for a brief period after saccade landing.
source: Assuming that orientation information was sampled simultaneously from the foveal and peripheral attentional focus, and assuming that the foci persisted for a brief period after saccade landing (Golomb, 2019; Jonikaitis et al., 2013)
evidence: Based on speculation supported by citations to Golomb, 2019; Jonikaitis et al., 2013

claim: The salient post-saccadic foveal view of the target may have allowed even early and therefore subthreshold pre-saccadic foveal information to contribute to an above-threshold signal.
source: the salient post-saccadic foveal view of the target may have allowed even early and therefore subthreshold pre-saccadic foveal information to contribute to an above-threshold signal.
evidence: Based on speculation about mechanism

claim: The joint modulation mechanism falls short of accounting for some aspects of the findings.
source: Nevertheless, this mechanism falls short of accounting for some aspects of our own as well as previous findings.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results

claim: Whether feature-based attention can operate at the level of complex shapes and whether the proposed mechanism is viable for naturalistic objects involving feature conjunctions is unclear.
source: Third, foveal retinotopic cortex contributes to the processing of complex peripheral shapes (Williams et al., 2008; Fan et al., 2016; Chambers et al., 2013; Yu and Shim, 2016; Weldon et al., 2020). Whether feature-based attention can operate at this level of abstraction, and whether the proposed mechanism is viable for naturalistic objects involving feature conjunctions, is unclear.
evidence: Based on inference and speculation about mechanism limitations

claim: The fovea's unique characteristics seem to be harnessed in a way that would not be viable at other visual field locations.
source: Consequently, the fovea may not merely be one of many locations an attention pointer can be allocated to. Instead, its unique characteristics seem to be harnessed in a way that would not be viable at other visual field locations.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results

claim: Temporal areas encode complex shapes, a coarse sketch of which could be fed back to foveal retinotopic cortex.
source: Moreover, temporal areas encode complex shapes, a coarse sketch of which could be fed back to foveal retinotopic cortex (Bullier, 2001).
evidence: Based on speculation supported by citation to Bullier, 2001

claim: Feedback delays to foveal retinotopic cortex would lie well within the range of typical saccade latencies.
source: Feedback delays to foveal retinotopic cortex would thus lie well within the range of typical saccade latencies (Becker, 1972).
evidence: Based on inference supported by citation to Becker, 1972

claim: Maximum enhancement was observed when the foveal probe appeared 150–200ms after the target.
source: Our results are consistent with this timing: we observed maximum enhancement when the foveal probe appeared 150–200ms after the target.
evidence: Based on experimental data from Experiment 1

claim: Saccades automatically establish a transient connection between the current and future foveal location.
source: These findings support the main assumption motivating the current study: saccades automatically establish a transient connection between the current and future foveal location, that is, the saccade target and the pre-saccadic center of gaze.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results and previous literature

claim: A similar connection between foveal and peripheral input may exist or be inducible by task demands during fixation.
source: A similar connection between foveal and peripheral input may exist or be inducible by task demands during fixation.
evidence: Based on speculation

claim: The connection between foveal and peripheral input is strengthened considerably when a saccade successively projects two otherwise unrelated visual field locations onto the same retinal location.
source: Arguably though, this connection is strengthened considerably when a saccade successively projects two otherwise unrelated visual field locations (the current center of gaze and the saccade target) onto the same retinal location (the fovea).
evidence: Based on inference about mechanism

claim: If foveal congruency effects rely on feedback connections, some selection mechanism is required that determines which object or object feature is processed in temporal areas and subsequently fed back to foveal cortex.
source: If foveal congruency effects rely on feedback connections, some selection mechanism is required that determines which object or object feature is processed in temporal areas and subsequently fed back to foveal cortex.
evidence: Based on inference about mechanism requirements

claim: During saccade preparation, the selection mechanism would emerge naturally through pre-saccadic attention shifts to the eye movement target.
source: During saccade preparation, this selection mechanism would emerge naturally: pre-saccadic attention shifts to the eye movement target in an obligatory fashion (Deubel and Schneider, 1996; Moore and Fallah, 2001) and transiently prioritizes the target over any other location in the visual field.
evidence: Based on inference supported by citations

claim: Pre-saccadic attention is a natural relevancy filter.
source: Most importantly, pre-saccadic attention is a natural relevancy filter – in spontaneous visual behavior, gaze is directed to the currently most significant object in the scene (Einhäuser et al., 2008; Nuthmann and Henderson, 2010; 't Hart et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on inference supported by citations

claim: Pre-saccadic attention may be potent enough to shape feedforward processing such that most of visual cortex is occupied with the processing of saccade target features at the moment the feedback mechanism is engaged.
source: All these properties identify pre-saccadic attention as a parsimonious and naturally emerging selection mechanism that may even be potent enough to shape feedforward processing: at the moment the feedback mechanism is engaged, most of visual cortex may indeed be occupied with the processing of saccade target features.
evidence: Based on speculation about mechanism

claim: Sufficient selection can likely be achieved through purely covert attention in the absence of eye movements, but feedback effects are expected to emerge more slowly.
source: Sufficient selection can likely be achieved through purely covert attention in the absence of eye movements. Nonetheless, feedback effects are expected to emerge more slowly (Rolfs and Carrasco, 2012). This is indeed what we observe.
evidence: Based on inference supported by citation and experimental results

claim: Foveal feedback during fixation may reflect the automatic preparation of an eye movement that is simply not executed.
source: It has been suggested that foveal feedback during fixation reflects the automatic preparation of an eye movement that is simply not executed (Fan et al., 2016; Chambers et al., 2013; Yu and Shim, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fan et al., 2016; Chambers et al., 2013; Yu and Shim, 2016

claim: Feedback effects would emerge during fixation inasmuch as the respective task engages the saccadic system.
source: In this case, feedback effects would emerge during fixation inasmuch as the respective task engages the saccadic system.
evidence: Based on inference from hypothesis about feedback mechanism

claim: The features of the target were made as task-irrelevant as possible to ensure that potential congruency effects would be automatic and not induced by a peripheral discrimination task.
source: Our paradigm likely covers the conservative end of this spectrum: we intentionally made the features of the target as task-irrelevant as possible, contrary to previous investigations. We intended to ensure that potential congruency effects would be automatic and not induced by a peripheral discrimination task.
evidence: Based on description of experimental design

claim: Increasing the conspicuity of the target by reducing its eccentricity or transparency against the background noise would trigger the saccadic system to a larger extent and thereby boost congruency effects during fixation.
source: It is conceivable that increasing the conspicuity of the target by reducing its eccentricity or transparency against the background noise would trigger the saccadic system to a larger extent and thereby boost congruency effects during fixation.
evidence: Based on speculation about potential manipulations

claim: Strong evidence that foveal prediction serves saccade preparation and spills over to fixation tasks would be provided if oculomotor characteristics of individual observers influence properties of the foveal congruency effect even during passive fixation.
source: In general, strong evidence that foveal prediction serves saccade preparation and, due to existing neuronal connections, spills over to any fixation task would be provided if the oculomotor characteristics of individual observers (such as their typical saccade latency) influence properties of the foveal congruency effect (such as its time course) even during passive fixation (Rolfs and Schweitzer, 2022).
evidence: Based on speculation supported by citation to Rolfs and Schweitzer, 2022

claim: Enhancement was aligned to the center of gaze irrespective of individual saccade endpoints, indicating findings are not a simple correlate of predictive remapping.
source: Since enhancement was aligned to the center of gaze irrespective of individual saccade endpoints, we conclude that our findings are not a simple correlate of predictive remapping (Collins et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results and citation to Collins et al., 2009

claim: Pre-saccadic foveal enhancement was more pronounced than its equivalent during fixation, suggesting that bottom-up covert attention shifts cannot account for the results.
source: Moreover, pre-saccadic foveal enhancement was more pronounced than its equivalent during fixation, suggesting that bottom-up covert attention shifts cannot account for our results.
evidence: Based on inference from comparison of Experiment 1 and Experiment 3

claim: Foveal enhancement does not seem to be a mere consequence of sensory information accumulation.
source: For similar reasons, foveal enhancement does not seem to be a mere consequence of sensory information accumulation: while the presentation duration of the target in the fixation condition was equal to the presentation duration of the saccade target in Experiments 1 and 2, congruency effects differed markedly.
evidence: Based on inference from comparison of experiments

claim: Enhancement did not increase monotonically across the target presentation period.
source: Furthermore, enhancement did not increase monotonically across the target presentation period. Especially in the PRE-only condition (Figure 4A), congruency effects were most pronounced in medium stages of saccade preparation, in accordance with established neuronal feedback latencies, and vanished in later stages.
evidence: Based on experimental data from Experiment 1

claim: The findings reflect perceptual enhancement rather than a shift in decision criterion.
source: Similar arguments support the notion that our findings reflect perceptual enhancement rather than a shift in decision criterion.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple lines of evidence

claim: A criterion shift would have affected HRs and FARs alike.
source: A criterion shift would have affected HRs and FARs alike.
evidence: Based on knowledge of signal detection theory

claim: The time course of enhancement during saccade preparation and fixation mirrored the typical temporal development of visual sensitivity during pre-saccadic attention shifts and covert attentional allocation, respectively.
source: Crucially, the time course of enhancement during saccade preparation and fixation mirrored the typical temporal development of visual sensitivity during pre-saccadic attention shifts and covert attentional allocation, respectively (Li et al., 2021; Rolfs and Carrasco, 2012).
evidence: Based on comparison to literature supported by citations to Li et al., 2021; Rolfs and Carrasco, 2012

claim: A defining feature of innately perceptual effects is their spatial specificity whereas criterion shifts should manifest in a spatially global fashion.
source: It has furthermore been argued that a defining feature of innately perceptual effects is their spatial specificity whereas criterion shifts should manifest in a spatially global fashion (Fritsche et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fritsche et al., 2017

claim: Model-based simulations suggest that attentional effects commonly interpreted as changes in perceptual sensitivity could be explained equally well by assuming localized variations of criterion.
source: Model-based simulations suggest that attentional effects commonly interpreted as changes in perceptual sensitivity could be explained equally well by assuming localized variations of criterion.
evidence: Based on inference from literature

claim: The findings would require an interplay between spatially specific and feature specific criterion shifts to be explained by criterion changes.
source: A decisive difference between the nature of criterion shifts in these simulations and our findings is that, while the simulated criterion changes would affect any visual information presented at a certain visual field location, our results would require an interplay between spatially specific and feature specific criterion shifts.
evidence: Based on inference from comparison to simulation literature

claim: Variations in criterion that are temporally, spatially and feature selective, follow the time course of pre-saccadic or covert attention, do not remain effective throughout an entire trial, are sensitive to the mean remapped target location, and do not affect parafoveal stimuli even after opacity adjustment would be unprecedented in the literature.
source: Variations in criterion that are temporally, spatially and feature selective, follow the time course of pre-saccadic or covert attention depending on observers' oculomotor behavior, do not remain effective throughout an entire trial, are sensitive to the mean remapped target location across trials, and do not affect parafoveal stimuli even after their opacity has been increased to match foveal performance would be unprecedented in the literature
evidence: Based on inference from literature review

claim: The continuous decrease in congruent and incongruent HRs across the saccade preparation period may reflect a gradually increasing decision criterion rather than a decrease in foveal visual sensitivity.
source: Similarly, we consider it unlikely that the overall HR time course relies on a temporal shift in criterion. More specifically, the continuous decrease in congruent and incongruent HRs across the saccade preparation period may reflect a gradually increasing decision criterion rather than a decrease in foveal visual sensitivity.
evidence: Based on speculation about alternative explanation

claim: A parsimonious explanation of the findings is that pre-saccadic foveal sensitivity decreases as attention shifts from the current center of gaze to the saccade target.
source: A parsimonious explanation of these findings and our data pattern is therefore that pre-saccadic foveal sensitivity decreases as attention shifts from the current center of gaze to the saccade target.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results and comparison to literature

claim: On a small subset of trials, participants have the strong impression of perceiving the target in the pre-saccadic center of gaze.
source: Lastly, we would like to share a phenomenological impression that was spontaneously reported by 6 out of 7 observers in Experiment 1 and experienced by the author L.M.K. many times. On a small subset of trials, participants in our paradigms have the strong impression of perceiving the target in the pre-saccadic center of gaze.
evidence: Based on phenomenological reports from observers

claim: The actual saccade target and its foveal equivalent are perceived simultaneously in different spatiotopic locations.
source: Interestingly, the actual saccade target and its foveal equivalent are perceived simultaneously in different spatiotopic locations, suggesting that this percept cannot be ascribed to a temporal misjudgment of saccade execution (after which the target would have actually been foveated).
evidence: Based on phenomenological reports from observers

claim: Foveal processing is optimized for surface features such as orientation, SF and color.
source: On the one hand, foveal processing is optimized for surface features such as orientation, SF and color, and may be recruited for the peripheral processing of primarily those properties.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about foveal processing

claim: During saccade preparation, any visual information at the eye movement target will be processed foveally upon landing.
source: On the other hand, and during saccade preparation in particular, any visual information at the eye movement target will be processed foveally upon landing.
evidence: Based on inference about visual processing during saccades

claim: The prediction of all visual features, even those for which foveal processing bares no significant advantage over peripheral processing, appears adaptive.
source: In consequence, the prediction of all visual features, even those for which foveal processing bares no significant advantage over peripheral processing (such as temporally modulated signals, McKee and Nakayama, 1984), appears adaptive.
evidence: Based on speculation supported by citation to McKee and Nakayama, 1984

claim: Ocular following upon saccade landing in response to coherent motion at the saccade target may well rely on foveal prediction.
source: Coherent motion at the saccade target, for instance, causes immediate ocular following upon saccade landing (Kwon et al., 2019), a response that may well rely on foveal prediction.
evidence: Based on speculation supported by citation to Kwon et al., 2019

claim: The feedback mechanism seems capable of operating at the complexity of feature conjunctions.
source: The feedback mechanism itself seems capable of operating at this complexity: high-level peripheral information such as object category has been successfully decoded from foveal neuronal activation (Williams et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on inference supported by citation to Williams et al., 2008

claim: How fed-back information interacts with high-contrast feedforward foveal input in naturalistic environments remains to be established.
source: Nonetheless, how fed-back information interacts with high-contrast feedforward foveal input – as it is likely required to when gaze is spontaneously directed from one object of interest to another – remains to be established.
evidence: Based on acknowledgment of limitation

claim: The pre-saccadic decrease in foveal sensitivity may boost the relative strength of fed-back signals by reducing the conspicuity of foveal feedforward input.
source: The pre-saccadic decrease in foveal sensitivity demonstrated previously as well as in our own data (Figure 2B) may boost the relative strength of fed-back signals by reducing the conspicuity of foveal feedforward input.
evidence: Based on speculation about mechanism

claim: Previous investigations on foveal feedback required observers to make peripheral discrimination judgments.
source: As stated above, previous investigations on foveal feedback required observers to make peripheral discrimination judgments.
evidence: Based on knowledge of previous literature

claim: Detecting the target was necessary to perform the oculomotor task in the current study.
source: We, in contrast, did not ask observers to generate a perceptual judgment on the orientation of the saccade target. Instead, detecting the target was necessary to perform the oculomotor task.
evidence: Based on description of experimental design

claim: The identification of local contrast changes would have sufficed to direct the eye movement.
source: While the identification of local contrast changes would have sufficed to direct the eye movement, the orientation of the target enhanced foveal processing of congruent orientations.
evidence: Based on inference about task requirements

claim: The automatic nature of foveal enhancement showcases that perceptual and oculomotor processing are tightly intertwined in active visual settings.
source: The automatic nature of foveal enhancement showcases that perceptual and oculomotor processing are tightly intertwined in active visual settings
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results

claim: Planning an eye movement appears to prioritize the features of its target.
source: planning an eye movement appears to prioritize the features of its target
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results

claim: Commencing the processing of target features before the eye movement is executed may accelerate post-saccadic target identification and provide a head start for corrective gaze behavior.
source: commencing the processing of these features before the eye movement is executed may accelerate post-saccadic target identification and ultimately provide a head start for corrective gaze behavior (Deubel et al., 1982; Ohl and Kliegl, 2016; Tian et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on speculation supported by citations to Deubel et al., 1982; Ohl and Kliegl, 2016; Tian et al., 2013

claim: The foveation of peripheral input via an eye movement may not merely be another instance of foveal feedback, but the very reason for its existence.
source: Since we routinely direct our gaze to relevant information rather than inspecting it peripherally, the foveation of peripheral input via an eye movement may not merely be another instance of foveal feedback, but the very reason for its existence.
evidence: Based on speculation about evolutionary function

claim: Seven human observers participated in Experiment 1.
source: Seven human observers (five females, seven right-handed, four right-eye dominant, one author) aged 22–34 years (Mdn = 28.0) participated in Experiment 1
evidence: Based on description of sample

claim: Nine observers participated in Experiment 2, six of whom had completed Experiment 1.
source: Nine observers, six of whom had completed Experiment 1, participated in Experiment 2 (seven females, all right-handed, seven right-eye dominant, no authors; 22–34 years, Mdn = 28.9).
evidence: Based on description of sample

claim: Seven observers participated in Experiment 3, five of whom had completed Experiment 1.
source: Seven observers, five of whom had completed Experiment 1, participated in Experiment 3 (five females, all right-handed, six right-eye dominant, one author; 23–36 years, Mdn = 29.0).
evidence: Based on description of sample

claim: The study complied with the Declaration of Helsinki in its latest version.
source: The study complied with the Declaration of Helsinki in its latest version and was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Department of Psychology at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin (reference number: 2018–09).
evidence: Based on statement of ethical compliance

claim: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Department of Psychology at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin.
source: The study complied with the Declaration of Helsinki in its latest version and was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Department of Psychology at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin (reference number: 2018–09).
evidence: Based on statement of ethical approval

claim: The research question, experimental paradigm and data analyses were preregistered on the Open Science Framework.
source: The research question, experimental paradigm and data analyses were preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/xr2jk and https://osf.io/6s24m).
evidence: Based on statement of preregistration

claim: Pre-processed data and experimental code are publicly available at https://osf.io/v9gsq/.
source: Pre-processed data and experimental code are publicly available at https://osf.io/v9gsq/.
evidence: Based on statement of data availability

claim: Stimuli were projected on a 200x113 cm screen using a PROPixx DLP Projector with a spatial resolution of 1920x1080 pixels and a refresh rate of 120 Hz.
source: Stimuli were projected on a 200x113 cm screen (Celexon HomeCinema, Tharston, Norwich, UK) using a PROPixx DLP Projector (Vpixx Technologies, Saint-Bruno, QC, Canada) with a spatial resolution of 1920x1080 pixels and a refresh rate of 120 Hz (frame duration of 8.3ms).
evidence: Based on description of apparatus

claim: Observers faced the screen at a viewing distance of 180 cm.
source: Observers faced the screen at a viewing distance of 180 cm while their heads were stabilized on a chin rest.
evidence: Based on description of apparatus

claim: The position of the dominant eye was recorded at a sampling rate of 1 kHz using a desk-mounted infrared eyetracker.
source: The position of the dominant eye was recorded at a sampling rate of 1 kHz using a desk-mounted infrared eyetracker (EyeLink 1000 Plus; SR Research, Osgoode, Canada).
evidence: Based on description of apparatus

claim: Across all 833 images presented in Experiment 1, the power spectral density decreased by 5.07 dB/octave.
source: Across all 833 images presented in the Experiment 1 (7 observers x7 sessions x17 images in the main experiment), the power spectral density (PSD) decreased by 5.07 dB/octave (Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on analysis of stimulus properties

claim: Across all 2205 images presented in the main experiment of Experiment 2, the power spectral density decreased by 4.89 dB/octave.
source: Across all 2205 images presented in the main experiment (9 observers x7 sessions x35 images), the power spectral density (PSD) decreased by 4.89 dB/octave.
evidence: Based on analysis of stimulus properties

claim: In Experiment 1, 8.12% of trials were excluded due to recorded gaze behavior not meeting certain requirements.
source: In offline analyses of Experiment 1, we excluded 8.12% of trials in which the recorded gaze behavior did not meet certain requirements (see Supplements).
evidence: Based on description of data exclusion

claim: In Experiment 1, a further 4.62% of trials were excluded in which the foveal probe disappeared intra- or post-saccadically rather than before saccade onset.
source: We excluded a further 4.62% of trials in which the foveal probe disappeared intra- or post-saccadically rather than before saccade onset.
evidence: Based on description of data exclusion

claim: A total of 27,328 trials from Experiment 1 were carried on to further analyses.
source: A total of 27,328 trials were carried on to further analyses.
evidence: Based on description of included data

claim: In Experiment 2, 11.25% of trials were excluded due to saccade characteristics.
source: In Experiment 2, we excluded 11.25% of trials due to saccade characteristics and a further 2.29% due to intra- or post-saccadic probe presentations.
evidence: Based on description of data exclusion

claim: In Experiment 2, a further 2.29% of trials were excluded due to intra- or post-saccadic probe presentations.
source: In Experiment 2, we excluded 11.25% of trials due to saccade characteristics and a further 2.29% due to intra- or post-saccadic probe presentations.
evidence: Based on description of data exclusion

claim: In Experiment 2, 0.89% of trials were excluded in which the target had been visible after saccade landing.
source: We furthermore excluded trials in which the target had been visible after saccade landing (0.89% of trials).
evidence: Based on description of data exclusion

claim: A total of 31,674 trials from Experiment 2 were carried on to further analyses.
source: A total of 31,674 trials were carried on to further analyses.
evidence: Based on description of included data

claim: In Experiment 3, 3.04% of trials were excluded in which observers had executed a microsaccade or a saccade before target offset.
source: In Experiment 3, we excluded 3.04% of trials in which observers had executed a microsaccade (amplitude ≤ 1.0 dva) or a saccade (amplitude >1.0 dva) before target offset.
evidence: Based on description of data exclusion

claim: A total of 5,430 trials from Experiment 3 were carried on to further analyses.
source: A total of 5,430 trials were carried on to further analyses.
evidence: Based on description of included data

claim: On each FA trial, a mean of 9.2 noise images had been visible for their full duration during the entire potential probe presentation period.
source: On each trial, we determined the noise images that had been visible for their full duration during the entire potential probe presentation period, that is, from the onset of the dynamic noise stream to the onset of the saccade (mean n=9.2).
evidence: Based on analysis of noise images

claim: Saccades were detected offline using a velocity-based saccade detection algorithm.
source: Saccades were detected offline using a velocity-based saccade detection algorithm (Engbert and Mergenthaler, 2006).
evidence: Based on description of analysis method and citation to Engbert and Mergenthaler, 2006

claim: Saccade onset was defined as the time point at which the current eye velocity had exceeded the median eye velocity from all preceding samples by 5 SDs for at least 8ms.
source: We defined saccade onset as the time point at which the current eye velocity had exceeded the median eye velocity from all preceding samples by 5 SDs for at least 8ms.
evidence: Based on description of analysis method

claim: Post-saccadic oscillations recorded with pupil-based eye trackers are assumed to reflect residual pupil movement rather than a true rotation of the eyeball.
source: When recorded with pupil-based eye trackers, saccades often exhibit post-saccadic oscillations, which are assumed to reflect residual pupil movement rather than a true rotation of the eyeball (Nyström et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nyström et al., 2013

claim: Post-saccadic oscillations were effectively excluded from the saccadic profile by not merging detected saccadic events separated by one sample or more.
source: We effectively excluded them from the saccadic profile by not merging detected saccadic events separated by one sample or more.
evidence: Based on description of analysis method
